newsitem.title: SOMALIA: Somali leaders slam Belgian soldiers' acquittal.
newsitem.headline: Somali leaders slam Belgian soldiers' acquittal.

text.p: Leaders from Somalia's two leading factions on Tuesday condemned the acquittal of two Belgian ex-paratroopers on charges of maltreating a Somalia child during a humanitarian mission in the African country in 1993.
The officials, from Ali Mahdi Mohamed's faction which controls north Mogadishu and from Hussein Aideed who controls the south, said they were outraged by the verdict of a Belgian court on Monday.

"The Belgians are still stuck with their discrimination policy. The acquittal of the two criminal soldiers was largely expected since European laws can never be just for Africans," Mohamed Qanyare Afrah, a senior official in Aideed's faction, told Reuters.
Qanyare said the behaviour of Belgian soldiers in Somalia had worked against its proclaimed humanitarian mission.
Hussein Sheikh Ahmed Kadare, an aide to Ali Mahdi, said the decision was a violation of international law and a degradation of Islam.
"The case needs to be reviewed by a neutral court and Moslem scholars and judges should be present during the procedure," Kadare said.
He added: "The acquittal is a total violation of international law and a degradation of the dignity of Islam.
A Brussels military court acquitted the two ex-paratroopers because of insufficient evidence.

"It could not be established that physical violence had been inflicted," presiding judge Dirk Moereman said, adding that there also was no conclusive evidence that the child's life had been in danger. The men were given the benefit of the doubt.
Kurt Coelus and Claude Baert had been identified from a photograph in Belgian daily Het Laatste Nieuws earlier this year which appeared to show them swinging a boy over a camp fire.
The prosecutor had demanded one month's prison for Coelus, now in the Belgian Navy, and Baert who has left the army.

A separate case involving their Sergeant Dirk Nassel will be heard in September. He was also charged with threatening behaviour and physical violence while serving in the same multinational peacekeeping mission in Somalia.
Nassel is alleged to have made a Somali Moslem boy eat pork and drink salt water.

Coelus and Baert, members of the 3rd Paratroop Battalion, had told the court they had meant no harm. They had merely played a game by grabbing one of the children attracted by the warmth of the fire, proclaiming they would 'roast' it.
The men had been playing with Somali children all day, mainly out of boredom.

The court said there had been no conclusive evidence that the child's clothing had caught fire while it was being swung over the fire for 30 seconds to a minute. "(The child) did not call out or cry...it started as a game," Moereman said.
The court said the child had been treated roughly, but there had been no hostility.

It dismissed charges of racism and inhuman behaviour brought by the Belgian Centre for Equal Opportunities and the Fight Against Racism. It disallowed an application by the Centre the charges be upgraded to war crimes under the Geneva Convention.

The court said there was insufficient evidence that the two men had had racist motives, although there might have been a generally racist atmosphere in their battalion or among other United Nations troops in Somalia.
Charges of maltreating Somali children have been made against Canadian and Italian troops who also served for the United Nations in Somalia.

Somalia has been without central authority since 1991 after rebels overthrew late president Mohamed Siad Barre. But they soon turned their guns on each other in murderous battles which killed hundreds of thousands and laid waste to the country.
